title: SLO Handoff and Release Safety Playbook
content:
Context:
This playbook is a compact, operational-first guide for running SLO handoffs into release windows and ensuring release safety for model-serving and inference control plane changes. It focuses on the human and data handoffs between Product, Platform, Serving Runtime, SRE, and CS.

Why this exists:
- We see recurring near-miss incidents during model rollouts where SLO ownership and rollback triggers are ambiguous.
- Goal: reduce release-related reliability regressions by 70% over the next 3 quarters via clearer contracts and lightweight automation.

Primary objectives:
1) Define a small, machine-readable SLO contract that travels with every release (version + critical metrics + rollback criteria).
2) Create a 7-step handoff checklist for releases touching the serving runtime, routing, and caching layers.
3) Establish an on-call preflight window with automated canary signal checks and human confirmation.
4) Run three 50-day experiments to validate the protocol across different product teams.

Scope (in/out):
- In: model variant rollouts, routing policy changes, quantization toggles, cache invalidation logic, new load profiles that affect latency/throughput.
- Out: non-production experiments, infra-only kernel upgrades that do not touch inference APIs (those use separate infra runbook).

Roles & responsibilities:
- Release Owner (Product/PM): owns the release checklist completion, priority, and customer comms.
- Platform Release Lead (platform-engineering): ensures infra preflight and capacity reservations are complete.
- Serving Runtime Lead (serving-runtime): verifies model serving telemetry and KV cache compatibility.
- SRE Gatekeeper (site-reliability-engineering): approves go/no-go based on SLO gates and incident budgets.
- CS/Support Rep: prepares customer-facing rollback comms and postmortem triage readiness.

The SLO Contract (deliverable):
- Version tag: string (e.g., model-x-v3.1.0).
- Primary SLOs: list (p90 latency <= 120ms, success rate >= 99.8%, embedding throughput >= 6k/s).
- Canary metrics and sample size: boolean pass/fail thresholds tied to 1k canary requests over 15 minutes.
- Rollback triggers: explicit criteria (see examples below).
- Owner contact: oncall rotation + Slack handle.

Example rollback triggers (concrete):
- sustained p95 latency increase > 40% vs baseline for 15m AND error rate > 0.2%
- regression in model fidelity evals (production prompts) with >2% drop in top-1 accuracy for 30m
- loss of >10% of KV cache hit rate causing >2x token compute cost

7-step Handoff Checklist (to be completed in order):
1) Draft SLO Contract created and attached to release PR.
2) Metrics baseline snapshot (last 24h) taken and uploaded to the release doc.
3) Capacity reservation confirmed with Platform (GPU / node pool sizing).
4) Canary harness configured and smoke scripts defined.
5) SRE preflight scheduled (30–60 minutes before rollout).
6) CS escalation packet prepared (template present).
7) Go/no-go decision logged (SRE Gatekeeper sign-off).

Preflight & Canary Routine:
- Start preflight 60 minutes before scheduled rollout window.
- Run a 15-minute low-volume canary against the new variant with telemetry hooks enabled.
- Automated checks evaluate SLO contract: latency, error rate, cache hit rate, cost per token estimate.
- If automated checks fail, the release is paused and the Rollback Owner engages.
- If automated checks pass, SRE Gatekeeper performs human validation and signs off.

Communication and tooling:
- Dedicated Slack channel naming convention: #release-<service>-<version> (archived after release).
- Release doc template: include SLO contract block, action history, rollback rationale.
- Automation hooks: small webhook that posts canary results to the channel and to the release doc.

Success metrics (measure this quarterly):
- Reduction in release-related incidents (severity >= P1/P2) by 70% within 3 quarters.
- Time-to-detect for release regressions reduced by 50% (median).
- Percentage of releases with complete SLO contract >= 95%.

Three 50-day experiments (hypothesis-driven):
Experiment A — Platform-first: require Platform Release Lead to provision a guarded canary lane for all model rollouts. Hypothesis: provisioning reduces capacity-related failures.
Experiment B — SLO-as-Code: embed the SLO contract in the release PR and validate automatically. Hypothesis: machine-readable contracts reduce ambiguity and speed gate decisions.
Experiment C — CS-in-the-loop: require CS rep sign-off for releases impacting enterprise customers. Hypothesis: early CS involvement reduces customer-impacting rollbacks.

Risk register (top items):
- Ambiguous ownership: mitigation = mandatory owner field in SLO contract + escalation path.
- False positives in canary checks: mitigation = conservative thresholds + human review.
- Tooling gaps: mitigation = temporary manual checklist + roadmap to automation.

Quick release runbook (one-pagers):
- Abort checklist: immediate steps to take if an automated canary fails (stop rollout, switch traffic to previous variant, notify CS).
- Rollforward checklist: criteria required to resume rollout after a transient failure (postmortem stub, fixes deployed to canary).

Implementation timeline (12 weeks high level):
Week 1–2: Playbook review with stakeholders; finalize contract schema.
Week 3–4: Build lightweight SLO-as-Code validator and release PR template.
Week 5–6: Pilot Experiment A with two product teams.
Week 7–9: Iterate tooling based on pilot feedback; onboard Experiment B.
Week 10–12: Expand to full rollout for all model-serving releases; measure metrics and prepare post-experiment report.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Should the SLO contract be stored in Git or Confluence? (tradeoffs: discoverability vs atomicity with PR).
- Standardized sample size for canary checks across services? (current variance causes noisy signals).
- Automatic rollback vs human-in-the-loop for certain severity levels.

Next steps (immediate):
- Schedule 60-minute walkthrough with SRE + Platform + Serving Runtime (owner: Jordan Kim, target: 2026-06-04).
- Create the SLO contract JSON schema and attach to the release PR template (owner: Aisha Patel, target: 2026-06-11).
- Add the webhooks and small canary result poster to the Ops repo (owner: Diego Morales, target: 2026-06-18).

Appendix: minimal SLO contract example (text form):
version: model-x-v3.1.0
primary_slos: [p90_latency_ms<=120, success_rate_pct>=99.8]
canary_window: 15m
canary_sample: 1000
rollback_triggers: [p95_latency_delta_pct>40, error_rate_pct>0.2]
owner: jordan.kim@redwood.ai

Notes to self (scratch):
- Keep this playbook intentionally compact; many teams prefer checklists over long policies.
- Plan a 30-minute brown bag to walk through real past incidents and map them to the new playbook.
summary: A compact operational playbook that defines an SLO contract, a 7-step handoff checklist, preflight/canary procedure, roles, experiments, timeline, and immediate next steps to reduce release-related reliability regressions.
